Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee, my name is Abi Iverson. I am the Development Director for Coastal Kids Preschool in Damariscotta, ME.
I am here to testify in favor of LD 1469: An Act to Amend the Quality Rating System for Child
Care Services in Maine.
`Z9 Coastal Kids Preschool represents one of the few, at my last count 84 providers in Maine, to hold
both an MRTQ Level 5 status and accreditation from the National Association for the Education
of Young Children (NAEYC). This rating allows our families to access the full benefit for the Child Care Affordability Program as well as a double tax credit on their Maine income tax return.
We are the only program in Lincoln County to hold both MRTQ Level 5 Status and NAEYC
accreditation, and it is my understanding that reaching Level 5 status requires accreditation.
Expanding the definition of an accredited program will provide more families with access to these benefits, as well as recognize our local programs for the high-quality programming they are
already delivering.
I would also suggest that the sponsors consider including Pre-k programs offered at NEASCaccredited private schools. With the continuing need for more pre-k programs, I know of private
schools that are expanding to include Pre-k pro gramming. Most of these schools either currently
have or ultimately seek accreditation from the New England Association of Schools and
Colleges.
Thank you for your time and consideration today.

Thank you, Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee. My name is Amanda Collamore. l the distinct honor of representing House District 68, Pittsfield, Clinton, Burnham, and Troy. l
have come before you today to present LD 1469: An Act to Amend the Quality
Rating System for Child Care Services in Maine. This bill is a meaningful step toward
recognizing and rewarding the high standards of care and education provided by Maine's early childhood programs. This will also fix an unintended consequence of the
previous legislation that inadvertently left out nationally recognized accreditation, hurting
these providers and the families they serve.
This legislation would amend 22 MRSA �3737 to ensure that child care programs
accredited by nationally recognized organizations---such as the National Association for
the Education of Young Children (NAEYC), the National Association for Family Child Care, and the Council on Accreditation---as well as those that meet federal Head Start standards, are given the highest rating in Maine`s Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS).
In Maine, this system is known as Rising Stars for Quality. lt's designed to help families identify child care providers that meet certain benchmarks for quality and continuous improvement. The system includes five levels, with five stars representing the highest level of quality. Ratings are based on staff qualifications, curriculum, assessment practices, family engagement, and overall program quality. Financial incentives, including differential reimbursement and tax benefits, are tied directly to these ratings.
You may ask, "How does national accreditation fit into Rising Stars for ME?"

Right now, however, those additional standards are creating a gap. Some programs go
through extensive national accreditation processes--meeting or even exceeding the
state's benchmarks--but still don't receive the highest QRIS rating in Maine. That sends the wrong message to providers who are doing everything right, and creates confusion
and inequity for families.
This issue also has real implications for families. A Maine taxpayer who enrolls a child in
a program with a Star 5 rating is eligible for a double child care tax credit on their state income tax return. That's a meaningful benefit for working families. More information is available through Maine Revenue Services at tinyurl.com/2nhxby5e.
In addition, families receiving support through the Child Care Affordability Program, or
CCAP, also see significant benefits based on the QRIS rating of the provider they
choose. If they choose a Star 4 program, their parent fee is reduced by 10%. If they
choose a Star 5 program, they receive a 20% reduction. When a high-quality, nationally
accredited provider isn't recognized at that top level, families lose access to savings they would othenrvise qualify for--despite choosing a program that clearly meets high
'
standards.
Maine's child care providers are already going above and beyond. They're facing workforce shortages, rising costs, and increased expectations, all while providing
essential care and early learning. When they meet rigorous national standards, they
should be recognized and supported---not left in a bureaucratic limbo.
l'd like to propose a small amendment to this bill that would add programs accredited by
the National Montessori Association to the list of nationally recognized accrediting
bodies. A program I accidentally left out. These programs meet high national standards
and are also currently recognized accordingly in Maine's system.
I respectfully urge the committee to support this bill and the proposed amendment. Let's
align our state system with the standards we already value nationally, and make sure
families and providers alike get the credit and support they deserve.
Thank you, and l'd be happy to answer any questions.

l--low is Rising Stdrs for ME different from Child Care Licensing?
The State of Maine regulates the need for and provision of a license to operate a child care program. Licensing regulations set the minimum standards that ensure the basic health. safety, and developmental needs of children are being met. Participation in Rising Stars for
ME is intended to recognize and promote higher quality care and to support and reward
programs that engage in continuous quality improvement efforts to move up the Stars.
Both Child Care Licensing and Rising Stars for ME are administered by Maine's Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). but each is managed within a different division.
Licenses are issued and monitored by the Division of Licensing and Regulatory Services,
Child Care Licensing Unit. Rising Stars for ME is administered by the Office of Child and
Family Services (OCFS). Child Care Unit. The divisions will share information regarding a program's current licensing status and compliance history. but Child Care Licensing staff do
not make decisions about the Star Rating of a program. OCFS makes the final determination
on a program's Star rating and issues the appropriate certificate.
OCFS makes the final determination on a program's Star rating and issues the appropriate
certificate. Star ratings are valid for two years. unless a program no longer meets the standards for their assigned Star.
\X/hat if my program has a conditional license?
A conditional license is a type of license that "may be issued by the Department when the
licensee or applicant fails to comply with the applicable law and rules and. in thejudgment of the Commissioner, the best interest of the public would be so served by issuing a conditional license. The department shall specify in writing when and what corrections must
be made during the term of the conditional license" (see Child Care Licensing Rules).
Issuance of a conditional license will result in a temporary change to Restricted Status.
in the event this should happen, it is the program's responsibility to inform families of the change in status and to revise any publications used for marketing that refer to the program's participation in Rising Stars for ME.
A program given a Restricted Status will receive a written plan of corrections from Child
Care Licensing to resolve the non-compliance. Upon completion of the plan and/or determination that the program is in compliance, the program may update their application and be rated at a Star 2 or higher.

The following steps are the general process for enrolling a program with Rising Stars for ME:
1. Ensure that all direct service staff (including administrative staff who work with children) are members of the MRTQ Registry. Join the MRTQ Registry here.

\X/hat is the process for a site visit?
The purpose of this announced and mutually agreed upon visit by OCFS is to review and
assess the quality of child care being provided as well as compliance with Department rules
and policies. During an on-site review, OCFS will:
0 Review the selected documents from the E-Portfolio to validate the Program's self-
assessment completed during the Rising Stars for ME application:
0 Observe the program's typical daily activities. routines. and interactions between adults
and children relevant to the Rising Stars for ME Standards and requirements.
Programs are selected from a random list of programs with Step 2. 3, 4 or 5 ratings based on
geographic regions. This process is important in the continuing efforts to maintain integrity of all programs enrolled in Rising Stars for ME.
\X/hen a Program is selected for a site visit. OCFS will contact the Program to arrange a date
and time for the visit. and provide written notification announcing the site visit to the
program no less than 30 calendar days prior to the site visit. OCFS will advise the program what information and materials must be provided to the OCFS employee during the site visit and notify the program when to expect a written summary of the site visit. OCFS will send a
letter summarizing the site visit to the program within ten business days.

\></hat if the program does not agree with the Star rating from
OCFS?
Programs that believe their Star rating is incorrect, or who do not feel the Star rating granted by OCFS is accurate. may appeal the decision by requesting in writing an informal review by OCFS. If the program is not satisfied with the result of the informal review. they may request
an administrative hearing. The following policy is in place for this purpose:
A program must request an informal review and obtain a decision before requesting an
administrative hearing. if the program is dissatisfied with the informal review decision, the
program owner/operator may write to OCFS at the Department of Heaith and Human Services
to request a hearing provided he/she does so within ten (10) calendar days of the date of the Director's report on the Department's action. Subsequent appeal proceedings will be limited only to those issues raised during the informal review. The Office of Administrative Hearings shall notify the program in writing of the date, time, and place of the hearing, and shall designate a presiding officer. Programs will be given at least twenty (20) calendar days' advance notice of the hearing date. The hearing shall be held in conformity with the Maine Administrative Procedures Act, 5 M.R.S.A. �8001 et seq. and the Administrative Hearings
Regulations.

Re: LD 1469 - An Act to Clarify the Quality Rating System for Child Care Services in Maine

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services, thank you for the opportunity to provide information in support of LD 1469, An Act to Clarify the Quality Rating System for Child Care Services in Maine.

LD 1469 proposes modification of the requirements for Maine's Quality Rating and Improvement System (QRIS) to specify that any child care provider who meets national accreditation standards must receive the highest rating within the QRIS (known as Star 5).

OCFS is in support of deferring to the accreditation process of the national organizations and entities listed in this bill by providing the highest QRIS rating to providers that are accredited by one of these bodies. Currently, Head Start programs which meet national program standards and other child care programs that are nationally accredited are placed at a Star 5 rating only if they also meet the Maine standards for Star 3 and Star 4.

Prior to the recent update to QRIS, a child care provider that received national accreditation would receive the highest possible rating, but in the transition to the Rising Stars for ME program there were additional requirements for providers beyond national accreditation in order to reach the highest possible rating. Primarily these requirements center around credential requirements for teachers with the QRIS requiring that 50% of lead teachers reach a Level 5 or above on the Early Childhood Education Workforce Registry. OCFS has heard this feedback and believes that allowing providers to universally meet Star 5 requirements with accreditation is supportive of providers who are striving to meet evidence-based standards.

OCFS supports passage of LD 1469 and would encourage the Committee to vote ought to pass on this bill.

Please feel free to contact me if you have any questions during your deliberation of this bill.

Sincerely,

Bobbi L. Johnson, LMSW Director Office of Child and Family Services Maine Department of Health and Human Services

Testimony of Hannah Marshall In support of LD 1469: An Act to Amend the Quality Rating System for Child Care Services in
Maine
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Health and
Human Sen/ices Committee, my name is Hannah Marshall and I am the Executive Director of Space to Thrive. I am testifying in favor of LD 1469: An Act to Amend the Quality Rating System
for Child Care Services in Maine.
Space to Thrive is a non profit program serving children and families in Windham and Raymond.
We currently operate three sites focused on out-of-school time and will soon open a fourth
location for early childhood education.
All three of our current locations are nationally accredited through the Council on Accreditation,
the governing body who reviews out of school time programs. The accreditation process is a
rigorous and time consuming commitment to proving quality care and upholding the standards
set forth by COA. We compile and submit a body of evidence sharing policies, procedures,
handbooks, trainings, and other documentation to support our accreditation. The process
culminates with a multi-day visit by an expert reviewer who compares what we have provided
with our daily operations.
In theory, this national accreditation should align with the Quality Rating System to achieve a 5
Star Rating. However, we must separately meet additional standards set forth by Maine Roads
to Quality. The Star 5 requirements outside of the national accreditation include submitting proof of inclusion practices, an inclusion training, and--the most challenging--staff requirements. Per
the rule, "at least 50% of all staff working at least twenty hours per week are at least a level 3 on
the MRTQ Direct Care Career Lattice."
In preparation for this testimony, I went back through communications with the Rising Stars
Quality Specialist. At our last point of renewal, we initially did not meet the 50% average of a level 3. In order to work around this, we reclassified several staff to not count in our total
consideration in order to meet the average lattice level the state requires. This can be through changing their role to "Substitute" or "Other" so they won't be "counted." These alternative titles also disqualify staff from the wage stipend-after the renewal process is complete, their titles return to what they were prior in order for them to continue to be paid those wages.
We also had one staff who consistently worked 22 hours, as a level 1. She was a college
student working towards her degree, but because she had just started her educational path, she
was bringing down our average. The simplest solution was to ask her to reduce her working hours to fall below the 20-hour threshoId--a solution that is counterproductive when we are
already constantly struggling with workforce capacity and coverage.
I could provide several additional examples of work-arounds that are confusing, contradictory to the spirit of the rule, and downright silly. Each August when our renewal is due, I have to play

this game in order for our program to maintain our Star 5 rating. ln a perfect world, the staff
qualification requirements would not be a hardship. However, given the constraints of the
workforce and the wages we can afford to pay, achieving the standards is difficult--or
impossible.
Regardless of what our team looks like at any given moment, the quality of our program remains the same--our routines, systems, curriculum, and practices are founded in developmentally appropriate practices. Each of our sites has well-qualified and experienced leadership who provide ongoing coaching, feedback, and training to their site's staff. Nearly all of our staff are on a professional development track to work their way up the lattice levels in the coming years-we have one in the apprenticeship program, two enrolled in higher education through the
TEACH scholarship, and two others working on their credentials. We have learned alongside
many other programs that the only way to grow a qualified workforce is to invest in the educators who have a passion for this work who will continue to need more professional
development.
I urge you to support this bill to streamline the process and support quality child care throughout the state. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Beyond our program, the hoops we have to jump through and the challenges we face, the rule as it is structured now deters other programs from beginning the national accreditation process. l have spoken to other directors who are providing high quality care, but who are apprehensive about beginning the accreditation process when it is so much work and does not guarantee a
Star 5 rating. l can think of one conversation in particular where a director of a program in a rural area in Western Maine said, "Why would I go through that whole process knowing I would still be stuck at a 3?" The staffing requirements in rural areas are even more challenging to
meet.
When families enroll in our program, they are selecting us as a nationally accredited, 5-star,
quality program. V\fith this choice, they are eligible for the doubled child care tax credit. If programs cannot meet the staffing requirements, families lose out on this opportunity through no fault of their own.
The solution is simple-align the Quality Rating System with the national accreditation standards.
Hannah Marshall Executive Director, Space to Thrive Windham/Raymond director@windhamraymondsacc.com

Sara Perrigo Scarborough LD 1469
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and distinguished members of the Health and Human Services Committee, my name is Sara Perrigo and I am the Co-Director of Heidi's House Child Care Center in Scarborough.
I am testify in favor of LD 1469: An Act to Amend the Quality Rating System for Child Care Services in Maine. We are an accredited center through the NAEYC (National Association for the Education of Young Children). We have maintained our accreditation for the last 18 years. We have no problems meeting all the standards to be a 5 Star program on the Quality Rating System for Child Care Services in Maine, however, the requirement to have all 50% of the staff at a level 5 or above is quite difficult to meet and maintain due to the significant struggles to hire teachers. We were barely able to meet it last year and it could be the only thing that keeps us from earning 5 stars the next time we renew. This has been frustrating as it is something we have little control over. I have worked as a Center Director for the past 25 years and have never seen such a shortage of qualified applicants (or any applicants) as I have in the last 3 years. Since the pandemic it is at a point where it continually impacts our ability keep our child care center open. We have a waitlist for every age group, yet we have classrooms that are only partially filled because we cannot hire qualified teachers. We work very hard to have a strong benefits package (including vacation time, personal time, health insurance, vision and dental insurance, 401K with a match, gym membership reimbursement, quarterly bonuses, etc.) and we keep our compensation very competitive for the field. And yet, still we struggle to hire. The good news is that we do have an amazing team of teachers who are taking advantage of high quality ECE trainings and utilizing the TEACH program. We also have a number of teachers who have degrees in different fields and are newer to the ECE field, so unfortunately it will take several years for them to be able to move up the career lattice to get to a level 5. The ECE field tends to have a higher employee turn over rate than other professions so career lattices that take years to move up on don't help us. Maine, as well as the rest of the nation, are struggling to hire ECE teachers. In fact, there are less students enrolling in ECE degree programs and applying for jobs since the start of the pandemic. It is nearly impossible to hire at all, let alone someone with an ECE degree and prior experience. With this knowledge, it would seem that if we are able to meet all the qualifications to be a nationally accredited program, then the state of Maine could also remove that requirement from their 5 Star Quality Rating level for programs that are NAEYC Accredited. We appreciate your consideration and your time.

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and honorable members of the Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is Whitney Files and I'm the CEO at the Penobscot Bay YMCA in Rockland and Rockport. I support LD 1469: An Act to Clarify the Quality Rating System for Child Care Services in Maine.
At the Penobscot Bay YMCA, we are proud to be the largest provider of child care in Knox County. Across our three early childhood centers, we care for children ages 6 weeks through 5 years with full-day, year-round programming from 7AM to 5PM.
We are especially proud to be one of only three programs in Knox County to hold a 5-star rating within Maine's Rising Stars for ME quality system. And we have also been nationally accredited through the National Association for the Education of Young Children (NAEYC) for nearly 15 years.
NAEYC accreditation is a gold standard in early childhood education. Achieving and maintaining it requires comprehensive evaluation of curriculum, staff qualifications, family engagement, health and safety, and continuous quality improvement. It is not a simple box-checking exercise; it is a rigorous, ongoing demonstration of excellence. Our commitment to quality is already validated by this nationally respected process.

Requiring supervisors to invest additional time in a second, redundant accreditation process does not improve quality--it takes time away from direct support to children, families, and staff.
This bill offers a commonsense solution. LD 1469 supports what's best for Maine by recognizing the existing excellence of NAEYC-accredited programs, easing unnecessary administrative burdens on providers, and ensuring families can access the quality programs that they deserve--all while streamlining systems without compromising quality so more Maine children can thrive in top-tier programs.
